title: DAO & Governance Complete Guide
subtitle: Master Decentralized Governance from Basics to Advanced Frameworks

intro.title: Introduction to DAOs
intro.content:
DAOs (Decentralized Autonomous Organizations) represent a fundamental shift in how organizations are structured and governed. Unlike traditional companies with boards and executives, DAOs are governed entirely by their community through transparent, on-chain voting mechanisms.

In this comprehensive guide, you'll learn how DAOs work, how governance mechanisms enable collective decision-making, and how you can participate in shaping the future of protocols you use. We'll explore real governance systems powering billions of dollars in DeFi protocols, from simple token voting to complex veToken models.

governance_basics.title: Understanding DAO Governance
governance_basics.content: Before diving into specific tools and frameworks, it's essential to understand the core principles that make DAO governance work. These concepts form the foundation of every governance system in crypto.

what_is_dao.title: What is a DAO?
what_is_dao.content:
A DAO is an organization represented by rules encoded as smart contracts, controlled by its members rather than a central authority. Key characteristics include:

  • Transparent Rules: All governance rules are encoded in open-source smart contracts
  • Community Control: Token holders vote on all major decisions
  • Trustless Execution: Approved proposals execute automatically via smart contracts
  • Global Participation: Anyone can participate regardless of location or identity

Real Examples:

  • MakerDAO: Governs the DAI stablecoin protocol with $5B+ TVL
  • Uniswap DAO: Controls the largest DEX with $3B+ in treasury
  • Compound: Community governs $2B+ lending protocol

how_governance_works.title: How Governance Works
how_governance_works.content:
The typical DAO governance process follows these steps:

  1. Discussion: Community discusses ideas in forums (Discord, Discourse)
  2. Temperature Check: Off-chain poll to gauge interest (usually on Snapshot)
  3. Formal Proposal: Detailed proposal submitted on-chain or to Snapshot
  4. Voting Period: Token holders vote (typically 3-7 days)
  5. Quorum Check: Verify minimum participation threshold met
  6. Execution: If passed, proposal executes (on-chain) or team implements (off-chain)

Example Flow (Uniswap):

  1. Discuss in Governance Forum
  2. Temperature check on Snapshot (50K UNI needed to propose)
  3. On-chain proposal via Governor Bravo (2.5M UNI needed)
  4. 7-day voting period (40M UNI quorum required)
  5. 2-day timelock delay
  6. Automatic execution if passed

voting_mechanisms.title: Voting Mechanisms
voting_mechanisms.content:
Different DAOs use different voting systems, each with unique trade-offs:

Token-Weighted Voting (Most Common):

  • 1 token = 1 vote
  • Simple and transparent
  • Risk: Whales dominate decisions
  • Used by: Compound, Uniswap, Aave

Quadratic Voting:

  • Cost increases quadratically (1 vote = 1 token, 2 votes = 4 tokens, 3 votes = 9 tokens)
  • Reduces whale influence
  • More complex to implement
  • Available on: Snapshot (as an option)

Conviction Voting:

  • Vote weight increases the longer you hold your vote
  • Encourages long-term thinking
  • Used by: 1Hive, Commons Stack

Holographic Consensus:

  • Prediction markets determine which proposals get attention
  • Addresses voter fatigue
  • Used by: DAOstack

governance_tools.title: Governance Tools
governance_tools.content: Several platforms have emerged to facilitate DAO governance, each serving different needs from gasless voting to on-chain execution.

snapshot.title: Snapshot: Gasless Voting
snapshot.content:
Snapshot is the most popular off-chain voting platform, used by thousands of DAOs including Uniswap, Aave, and ENS.

Key Features:

  • Zero Gas Costs: Voting is completely free (uses signature-based voting)
  • Flexible Strategies: Support for various voting mechanisms (token balance, delegation, LP tokens)
  • Custom Plugins: Integration with Gnosis Safe, Discord, etc.
  • Multi-Chain: Works across Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum, and more

How It Works:

  1. DAO creates a Snapshot space with custom settings
  2. Token holders connect wallets to view proposals
  3. Voters sign messages (no gas) to cast votes
  4. Votes verified using blockchain state at specific block height
  5. Results tallied, but execution is manual (off-chain)

Limitations:

  • No automatic execution (results are non-binding)
  • Vulnerable to last-minute vote swings
  • Requires trust in implementation team

tally.title: Tally: On-Chain Governance
tally.content:
Tally provides a user-friendly interface for on-chain governance, primarily for Governor contracts (OpenZeppelin standard).

Key Features:

  • On-Chain Execution: Proposals automatically execute when passed
  • Governor Support: Works with Governor Alpha, Bravo, and OpenZeppelin Governor
  • Delegation Interface: Easy delegation of voting power
  • Analytics: Track voter participation, proposal success rates
  • Notifications: Get alerts for new proposals and vote reminders

How It Works:

  1. Connect wallet to Tally
  2. Browse DAOs using Governor contracts (Compound, Uniswap, Gitcoin)
  3. View active proposals with detailed descriptions
  4. Vote on-chain (costs gas)
  5. Monitor proposal status through voting, timelock, and execution

Advantages Over Snapshot:

  • Binding results with automatic execution
  • Higher legitimacy (on-chain verification)
  • Timelock delays prevent instant execution attacks

Disadvantages:

  • Voting costs gas (can be $10-100 on Ethereum)
  • Only works with Governor-compatible contracts

boardroom.title: Boardroom: Governance Aggregator
boardroom.content:
Boardroom aggregates governance activity across multiple DAOs, helping participants track and manage their voting power.

Key Features:

  • Multi-DAO Dashboard: See all your governance positions in one place
  • Protocol Coverage: Tracks 100+ DAOs across different platforms
  • Delegation Tracking: Monitor who's delegating to whom
  • Analytics: Deep insights into governance patterns
  • API Access: Programmatic access to governance data

Use Cases:

  • Delegates managing votes across multiple protocols
  • Researchers analyzing governance trends
  • DAOs benchmarking their governance activity

token_governance.title: Token-Based Governance
token_governance.content: Most DAOs use governance tokens to enable voting. Understanding how these tokens work is crucial for effective participation.

governance_tokens.title: Governance Tokens
governance_tokens.content:
Governance tokens grant holders the right to vote on protocol decisions. Unlike pure utility tokens, governance tokens represent ownership and control.

Examples of Major Governance Tokens:

  • UNI (Uniswap): 1B total supply, governs $3B+ treasury
  • COMP (Compound): 10M total supply, controls lending protocol parameters
  • AAVE: Controls Aave protocol and safety module
  • MKR (Maker): Governs DAI stablecoin system

What Governance Tokens Control:

  • Protocol parameters (fees, interest rates, collateral ratios)
  • Treasury spending (grants, partnerships, liquidity incentives)
  • Smart contract upgrades (within governance-controlled upgrade mechanisms)
  • Economic policies (token emission, buybacks, staking rewards)

Token Distribution:

  • Team/Founders: 20-30% (usually with vesting)
  • Investors: 10-20% (with vesting)
  • Community/Users: 40-60% (via liquidity mining, airdrops)
  • Treasury/DAO: 10-20% (for future initiatives)

delegation.title: Delegation
delegation.content:
Delegation allows token holders to assign their voting power to others without transferring ownership of tokens.

Why Delegate?

  • Don't have time to evaluate every proposal
  • Delegate to experts in specific domains
  • Improve governance efficiency (avoid proposal failures due to low quorum)
  • Earn reputation as a delegate

How Delegation Works:

  1. Token holder calls delegate(address) function
  2. Voting power transfers to delegate (tokens stay in your wallet)
  3. Delegate can vote with combined power from all delegators
  4. You can redelegate or vote yourself anytime

Famous Delegates:

  • a16z (Andreessen Horowitz): Major delegate in Uniswap, Compound, Aave
  • Gauntlet: Risk management firm, active in multiple DeFi DAOs
  • Flipside Crypto: Data analytics firm serving as delegate

Becoming a Delegate:

  1. Create delegate profile on platforms like Tally
  2. Share your governance philosophy and expertise
  3. Participate actively in discussions
  4. Vote consistently on proposals
  5. Publish voting rationale transparently

vetoken_models.title: veToken Models (Vote-Escrowed)
vetoken_models.content:
Vote-escrowed (ve) token models lock tokens for extended periods in exchange for enhanced voting power and rewards. Pioneered by Curve Finance.

How veCRV Works:

  • Lock CRV for up to 4 years → receive veCRV
  • 1 CRV locked for 4 years = 1 veCRV
  • 1 CRV locked for 1 year = 0.25 veCRV
  • veCRV decays linearly until lock expires

Benefits of Locking:

  • Boosted Rewards: Up to 2.5x boost on CRV emissions
  • Voting Power: Direct gauge weights (control CRV emissions to pools)
  • Protocol Revenue: Share of protocol fees
  • Governance Rights: Vote on protocol changes

The Curve Wars:

Protocols compete to accumulate veCRV to direct emissions to their pools:

  • Convex: Aggregates CRV, controls 50%+ of veCRV supply
  • Yearn: Holds significant veCRV position
  • Stake DAO: veCRV accumulation strategy

This created a meta-game where protocols bribe veCRV holders to vote for their pools, worth millions in incentives.

Other veToken Implementations:

  • veBAL (Balancer): 80/20 BAL/ETH LP locked
  • vlCVX (Convex): Locked CVX for voting on Curve gauges
  • veANGLE (Angle Protocol): Governance and fee sharing

treasury_management.title: Treasury Management
treasury_management.content: DAOs control billions in treasuries. Proper management requires secure multi-signature wallets and transparent fund flows.

multisig_wallets.title: Multi-Signature Wallets
multisig_wallets.content:
Multi-sig wallets require multiple signatures to execute transactions, providing security and decentralization.

Gnosis Safe (Most Popular):

  • M-of-N signature scheme (e.g., 3-of-5, 4-of-7)
  • Supports any transaction type (transfers, contract calls)
  • Transaction builder for complex interactions
  • Integration with DeFi protocols

Common Multi-Sig Configurations:

  • Small DAOs: 3-of-5 (quick decisions, moderate security)
  • Large DAOs: 6-of-9 or higher (more security, slower execution)
  • Emergency Response: 2-of-3 for time-sensitive actions

Who Are Signers?

  • Core team members
  • Elected community representatives
  • Security partners (e.g., white-hat hackers)
  • Legal entities (for regulatory compliance)

Real Examples:

  • Uniswap Treasury: 4-of-7 multi-sig managing $3B+
  • Compound: 9-of-13 community multi-sig
  • Gitcoin: 6-of-10 multi-sig for grants

Security Best Practices:

  • Geographic distribution (prevent single-point physical threats)
  • Hardware wallets for all signers
  • Regular signer rotation
  • Public announcement of signer changes
  • Timelock delays for large transactions

token_vesting.title: Token Vesting & Streaming
token_vesting.content:
Token vesting ensures team members and contributors receive tokens gradually over time, aligning long-term incentives.

Traditional Vesting:

  • 1-year cliff: No tokens released for first year
  • 4-year vesting: Tokens unlock linearly over 4 years
  • Example: 1M tokens with 1-year cliff, 4-year vest = 0 tokens year 1, then 250K/year for years 2-5

Sablier: Token Streaming Protocol:

  • Continuous Vesting: Tokens unlock every second, not in batches
  • Recipient Control: Withdraw unlocked tokens anytime
  • Sender Cancellation: Cancel stream and reclaim unvested tokens
  • DeFi Integration: Stream any ERC-20 token

Use Cases:

  • Team Compensation: Stream salaries in stablecoins or governance tokens
  • Grants: Progressive funding for contributors
  • Investor Unlocks: Transparent, verifiable vesting
  • Liquidity Mining: Stream rewards to LPs

Advantages Over Traditional Vesting:

  • Fairer: No cliff anxiety or sudden dumps
  • Transparent: On-chain verification of vesting schedule
  • Flexible: Recipients can withdraw as needed
  • Tax Efficient: Potentially better tax treatment in some jurisdictions

dao_frameworks.title: DAO Frameworks
dao_frameworks.content: Several frameworks exist to help create and manage DAOs, each optimized for different use cases.

aragon.title: Aragon
aragon.content:
Aragon is one of the oldest and most feature-complete DAO frameworks, allowing anyone to create and manage DAOs.

Key Features:

  • DAO Templates: Pre-built templates for common governance structures
  • Modular Apps: Add features via apps (voting, finance, tokens)
  • Permissions System: Granular control over who can do what
  • Aragon Court: Decentralized dispute resolution

Aragon Templates:

  • Company Template: Transferable token-based voting
  • Membership Template: Non-transferable membership shares
  • Reputation Template: Merit-based voting power

Notable Aragon DAOs:

  • Decentraland: Virtual world governance
  • API3: Decentralized API governance
  • BrightID: Social identity network

Recent Updates (Aragon OSx):

  • Modular plugin architecture
  • Multi-chain deployment (Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum)
  • Improved gas efficiency
  • Better developer experience

moloch.title: Moloch DAO
moloch.content:
Moloch pioneered a minimalist DAO design focused on grants and funding coordination, with a unique 'rage quit' feature.

Core Concepts:

  • Shares: Non-transferable voting shares
  • Loot: Non-voting economic shares
  • Proposals: Membership, funding, or trade proposals
  • Rage Quit: Exit with proportional treasury share anytime

How Moloch Works:

  1. Member submits proposal with tribute (payment)
  2. 7-day voting period (1 share = 1 vote)
  3. 7-day grace period (allows rage quit before execution)
  4. If passed, tribute goes to treasury, member receives shares

Why Grace Period + Rage Quit?

This protects minority holders from malicious proposals. If a bad proposal passes, minorities can exit with their funds before execution.

Moloch Variations:

  • Moloch v2: Added loot, trade proposals, GuildKick
  • Moloch v3 (Baal): Shaman (external contract) permissions, better UX
  • DAOhaus: No-code Moloch DAO launcher

Best For:

  • Grant-giving DAOs (e.g., MetaCartel, Moloch DAO itself)
  • Venture DAOs pooling capital
  • Communities prioritizing minority protection

compound_governor.title: Compound Governor (OpenZeppelin)
compound_governor.content:
The Governor contract, originally created by Compound and standardized by OpenZeppelin, is the most widely used on-chain governance framework.

Governor Evolution:

  • Governor Alpha: Original Compound governance
  • Governor Bravo: Added proposal cancellation, better gas efficiency
  • OpenZeppelin Governor: Modular, extensible standard

How It Works:

  1. Propose: Submit proposal with executable code (requires proposal threshold, e.g., 1% of supply)
  2. Vote: Token holders vote For/Against/Abstain
  3. Queue: If passed (quorum met, majority votes), proposal queued in Timelock
  4. Execute: After timelock delay (typically 2 days), anyone can execute

Key Parameters:

  • Proposal Threshold: Tokens needed to propose (prevents spam)
  • Quorum: Minimum votes needed for validity (prevents low-turnout attacks)
  • Voting Period: How long voting lasts (typically 3-7 days)
  • Timelock Delay: Delay before execution (emergency exit window)

Pros:

  • Battle-tested (Compound, Uniswap, Gitcoin, and 100+ protocols use it)
  • Automatic execution (no manual implementation needed)
  • Fully on-chain (highest legitimacy)

Cons:

  • High gas costs for voting
  • High barriers to entry (proposal threshold)
  • Complexity for users

Used By:

  • Compound ($2B TVL)
  • Uniswap ($3B TVL)
  • Gitcoin (grants platform)
  • Nouns DAO (NFT project with daily auctions)

participating.title: Participating in DAOs
participating.content: Active participation in governance is crucial for DAO success. Here's how to get involved effectively.

finding_daos.title: Finding DAOs to Join
finding_daos.content:
Where to Discover DAOs:

  • Snapshot Spaces: Browse 20,000+ DAOs at snapshot.org
  • Tally: Explore Governor-based DAOs at tally.xyz
  • Boardroom: DAO aggregator at boardroom.io
  • DeepDAO: DAO analytics at deepdao.io
  • DAOlist: Curated directory at daolist.io

Criteria for Selecting DAOs:

  • Alignment: Does the DAO's mission align with your values?
  • Activity: Are proposals regular and meaningful?
  • Participation: Is voter turnout healthy (>10%)?
  • Treasury: Does the DAO have sustainable funding?
  • Community: Is the Discord/forum active and welcoming?

Starting Small:

  1. Join DAO Discord/forum and observe
  2. Read past proposals to understand governance
  3. Participate in discussions before voting
  4. Start voting on smaller proposals
  5. Consider delegating to learn from experienced voters

voting_strategies.title: Voting Strategies
voting_strategies.content:
When to Vote:

  • High-Impact Proposals: Treasury spending >1% of funds, protocol parameter changes, smart contract upgrades
  • Your Expertise Area: Vote on proposals in domains you understand
  • Controversial Issues: Close votes need every participant

When to Abstain:

  • You don't fully understand the proposal
  • You have a conflict of interest
  • You want to help reach quorum without influencing outcome

Due Diligence Before Voting:

  1. Read Full Proposal: Don't vote on titles alone
  2. Check Discussion: What are experts saying?
  3. Verify Claims: Proposals may include inaccurate data
  4. Consider Externalities: What are unintended consequences?
  5. Review Code: For smart contract proposals, review or verify audit

Delegation Strategy:

  • Delegate to multiple specialists (if protocol allows)
  • Periodically review delegate voting history
  • Redelegate if delegate becomes inactive or votes contrary to your values

proposal_creation.title: Creating Proposals
proposal_creation.content:
Creating effective proposals is an art. Here's how to maximize your proposal's chances of passing.

Pre-Proposal Phase:

  1. Forum Discussion: Post initial idea in governance forum
  2. Gather Feedback: Incorporate community suggestions
  3. Find Supporters: Build coalition before formal proposal
  4. Estimate Costs: Provide detailed budget if requesting funds

Proposal Structure:

  • Title: Clear, descriptive (not clickbait)
  • Summary: One-paragraph overview for busy voters
  • Motivation: Why is this needed? What problem does it solve?
  • Specification: Detailed description of what will happen
  • Rationale: Why this approach over alternatives?
  • Implementation: Technical details, timeline, milestones
  • Budget: If requesting funds, itemized breakdown
  • Success Metrics: How will success be measured?

Common Proposal Types:

  • Parameter Changes: Adjust fees, interest rates, collateral ratios
  • Treasury Spending: Grants, partnerships, liquidity incentives
  • Protocol Upgrades: Add new features or fix bugs
  • Governance Changes: Modify voting rules or parameters
  • Meta-Governance: How the DAO should vote in other DAOs

Tips for Success:

  • Keep it simple (complex proposals scare voters)
  • Break large proposals into smaller chunks
  • Show track record (previous contributions help)
  • Be responsive to questions during voting
  • Accept that not every proposal will pass

risks.title: Governance Risks and Challenges
risks.content: DAO governance isn't perfect. Understanding the risks helps you participate more effectively and protect your interests.

governance_attacks.title: Governance Attacks
governance_attacks.content:
Several attack vectors threaten DAO governance:

1. Flash Loan Governance Attacks:

  • Attacker borrows massive amount of governance tokens via flash loan
  • Votes on malicious proposal
  • Returns tokens in same transaction
  • Defense: Snapshot voting power at previous block (before proposal)

2. Vote Buying:

  • Attacker buys or borrows enough tokens to pass malicious proposal
  • Extracts value, then sells tokens
  • Defense: Timelocks (give token holders time to exit), high quorum requirements

3. 51% Attacks:

  • Single entity accumulates majority voting power
  • Can pass any proposal unilaterally
  • Defense: Quadratic voting, delegation caps, veto power for minority

Real Attack Examples:

  • Beanstalk (April 2022): Attacker used flash loan to pass malicious proposal, stole $76M
  • Build Finance (Feb 2021): Hostile takeover via token buying, $470K drained

Warning Signs:

  • Proposals submitted late in voting period
  • Sudden large token transfers to new addresses
  • Proposals with minimal discussion
  • Unrealistic promises or emergency urgency

voter_apathy.title: Voter Apathy
voter_apathy.content:
Low voter participation is one of the biggest challenges facing DAOs.

The Problem:

  • Typical voter turnout: 5-15% of eligible tokens
  • Most holders are passive investors, not active governors
  • Voter fatigue from too many proposals
  • Complexity barrier (technical proposals hard to understand)

Consequences:

  • Small minority can control decisions
  • Proposals fail to reach quorum
  • Centralization risk (active voters accumulate power)
  • Delegated voters may not represent broad community

Solutions Being Tried:

  • Voting Incentives: Reward active voters (e.g., vote-escrowed models)
  • Delegation: Make it easy to delegate to active participants
  • Improved UX: Simplify voting interface and proposal summaries
  • Conviction Voting: Set-and-forget voting (stake stays voted until you change)
  • Prediction Markets: Let markets signal proposal outcomes

plutocracy_concerns.title: Plutocracy (Whale Dominance)
plutocracy_concerns.content:
Token-weighted voting naturally favors large holders, creating plutocratic governance.

The Reality:

  • Top 1% of holders often control >50% of voting power
  • VCs and early investors have disproportionate influence
  • Whales can override community consensus

Examples:

  • Uniswap: Top 10 addresses control ~40% of voting power
  • Compound: a16z alone can nearly reach quorum

Mitigation Strategies:

  • Quadratic Voting: Diminishing returns for larger stakes
  • Identity-Based Voting: One person = one vote (requires identity solution)
  • Multi-Chamber Governance: Separate houses for token holders and users
  • Rage Quit: Minority protection mechanism (Moloch DAOs)
  • Veto Power: Technical/security council can veto dangerous proposals

The Trade-off:

Token-weighted voting aligns incentives (large holders have most at stake) but can exclude smaller participants. There's no perfect solution—each DAO must choose based on its values and goals.

legal_uncertainty.title: Legal and Regulatory Uncertainty
legal_uncertainty.content:
DAOs exist in a legal gray area, creating risks for participants.

Key Questions:

  • Are DAOs legal entities?
  • Are token holders liable for DAO actions?
  • How are DAO treasuries taxed?
  • Are governance tokens securities?

Current Legal Landscape:

  • Wyoming (USA): Allows DAO LLCs (legal entity wrapper for DAOs)
  • Marshall Islands: DAO-specific legislation passed
  • Switzerland: DAO-friendly jurisdiction (many DAOs incorporate here)
  • Most Countries: No clear guidance yet

Notable Legal Issues:

  • Ooki DAO (2022): CFTC sued DAO directly, claiming token holders are liable
  • SEC Scrutiny: Governance tokens may be securities (Howey test)
  • Tax Uncertainty: How to report DAO income and voting?

Risk Management:

  • Legal Wrapper: Incorporate as LLC or foundation
  • Geographic Diversity: Multi-sig signers in different jurisdictions
  • Compliance: Consult lawyers on security law implications
  • Decentralization: More decentralized = harder to regulate
  • Documentation: Clear records of governance decisions

Disclaimer: This is not legal advice. Consult with a lawyer familiar with DAO regulations in your jurisdiction before participating in or creating DAOs.

dao.definition: An organization governed by smart contracts and community voting rather than centralized management. Rules are transparent and decisions are made collectively by token holders.

governance_token.definition: A token that grants holders voting rights in a DAO. Each token typically represents one vote, allowing holders to influence protocol decisions and parameter changes.

proposal.definition: A formal suggestion for action submitted to a DAO for voting. Proposals can include parameter changes, treasury spending, protocol upgrades, or governance modifications.

quorum.definition: The minimum number of votes required for a proposal to be valid. Prevents proposals from passing with very low participation. Typical quorum: 4-10% of total token supply.

delegation.definition: Assigning your voting power to another address without transferring token ownership. Allows token holders to participate in governance indirectly through trusted representatives.

timelock.definition: A delay between proposal approval and execution, typically 24-48 hours. Gives token holders time to exit if they disagree with a passed proposal, preventing instant attacks.

multisig.definition: A wallet requiring M-of-N signatures to execute transactions (e.g., 3-of-5). Provides security through distributed control, commonly used for DAO treasuries.

rage_quit.definition: A mechanism (popularized by Moloch DAO) allowing members to exit with their proportional share of treasury assets. Protects minorities from being exploited by majority votes.

vetoken.definition: Tokens locked for extended periods (up to 4 years) in exchange for voting power and boosted rewards. Pioneered by Curve Finance (veCRV), aligns long-term incentives.

quadratic_voting.definition: A voting system where cost increases quadratically with votes (1 vote = 1 token, 2 votes = 4 tokens). Reduces whale influence and gives smaller holders more relative power.
